title: edge proximity latency & cost snapshot
content:
Purpose
This note captures a compact, opinionated snapshot of experiments comparing "near-edge" PoPs (small regional points of presence) against core cloud regions for short-chat workloads. Goal: decide whether to prioritize additional near-edge capacity for PLG-hosted customers who report latency perceived on mobile in APAC/EU.

Summary (short)
- Method: synthetic chat workload (turns: 8–20 tokens output, 2–6 tokens input) replayed from recorded traffic (sampled user traces) across three regions: core (us-west-2), near-edge (equatorial PoP), and metro-edge (city PoP).
- Measurements: p50/p90/p99 latency (server-side), client-observed RTT (simulated mobile network profiles), and cost-per-1k-tokens (amortized GPU + networking uplift).
- Key finding: near-edge reduces client-observed p50 by ~35-45ms vs core for short-turn chats in high RTT markets at an incremental cost of 6–12% per request when accounting for smaller instance types and lower batching efficiency. p99 improvement is more modest and depends on warm caches.

Experimental setup
- Model: redwood-compact-v1 (decoder-only, 6B-ish) with single-shard GPU serving.
- Traffic shape: 60% short-turn (<=32 tokens), 30% mid-turn (32-128), 10% long-turn (>128).
- Concurrency: 1–8 concurrent sessions per instance to emulate PLG usage.
- Caching enabled: prefix KV caching ON for repeated prompts; cold-start fraction set to 12%.
- Batching policy: opportunistic small-window batching (window 8ms), with max batch size 16.
- Network profiles: mobile-good (40ms base RTT, 30% jitter), mobile-poor (120ms RTT, 50% jitter), broadband (12ms RTT).

Raw numbers (median of 5 runs)
- Core (us-west-2)
  server p50: 42ms | p90: 88ms | p99: 210ms
  client-observed p50 (mobile-good): 94ms | mobile-poor: 174ms
  cost per 1k tokens: $0.092

- Metro-edge (city PoP)
  server p50: 34ms | p90: 70ms | p99: 180ms
  client-observed p50 (mobile-good): 72ms | mobile-poor: 140ms
  cost per 1k tokens: $0.099

- Near-edge (small regional PoP)
  server p50: 28ms | p90: 64ms | p99: 172ms
  client-observed p50 (mobile-good): 58ms | mobile-poor: 128ms
  cost per 1k tokens: $0.103

Interpretation notes
- Absolute server-side p50 improvements are modest (14ms median between core and near-edge) because model runtime dominates token generation for these short outputs. However client-observed improvements are larger due to reduced network RTT and early ACKs for small responses.
- p99 still dominated by tail runtime events (cache miss + kernel contention). Near-edge reduces network tail but cannot eliminate large server-side stalls.
- Cost increase arises from: smaller GPUs with worse throughput per-dollar, lower batching (smaller windows), and additional overheads for multi-PoP orchestration (replicated control plane cost attributed). We amortized orchestration by assuming 20% cross-PoP spare capacity.

ASCII visualizations (sketches)
- Client p50 (mobile-poor) by region (ms):
  core       | ################################################# 174ms
  metro-edge | ########################################### 140ms
  near-edge  | ############################# 128ms

- Cost per 1k tokens ($):
  core       | ########################## $0.092
  metro-edge | ############################ $0.099
  near-edge  | ############################### $0.103

- Server p99 distribution (relative buckets):
  buckets (ms): 0-100 | 100-200 | 200-400 | 400+
  core       :  55%  |   30%   |   12%   | 3%
  near-edge  :  60%  |   28%   |   10%   | 2%

Tradeoffs and decision framing
- If product goal is to reduce perceived latency for mobile-first PLG adoption in high-RTT markets, near-edge has clear UX value. p50 reductions translate to faster perceived responses and likely conversion/repeat usage improvements.
- If goal is to minimize unit cost (hosted margins), near-edge is marginally worse. The extra 6–12% cost needs to be justified by measurable engagement delta.
- p99 improvements are insufficient if customers need hard tail SLOs; for that we should pursue runtime fixes (kernel scheduling, pre-warming) in parallel.

Recommendations (practical)
- Short term: enable a trial near-edge PoP for a small subset of traffic (canary 5% for targeted countries) with metrics instrumented: client p50/p90, session retention, cost delta per month. (Linked linear: EDGE-431)
- Medium term: experiment with micro-batching policy that increases batch window slightly for near-edge (trade client p50 +2–5ms for cost -3%). Measure impact on throughput and user metrics.
- Long term: invest in per-PoP kernel tuning and lightweight shard collocation (reduce cross-shard jitter). Also explore instance families with higher single-thread perf for short-turn chats.

Open questions / TODOs
- Need a clearer amortization model for control-plane replication costs across 20+ PoPs. Current 20% assumption is hand-wavy. Finance to model (ticket: FIN/OPS-118).
- Validate with real production traffic (we used sampled traces; privacy-safe conversion needed). Ask privacy for guidance on trace sampling (PR: github.com/redwood-inference/privacy/trace-sample#9).
- Run p99-focused microbenchmarks under adversarial load to confirm whether near-edge reduces server stalls at tail.

Appendix: quick configs used
- Serving: runtime v2.3-alpha, kernel set: fast-emu-1, batching: opportunistic-8ms, cache: kv-prefetch=on
- Instance types: core: p4d-like equivalent; near-edge: single-GPU a2-like; metro-edge: a2-highmem variant
- Measurement scripts: bench/replay_edge_snapshot.py (local), upload to artifact PR above

Notes to reviewers
- This is intentionally compact; I expect follow-ups with more rigorous cost model and production validation. Please flag any obvious omissions (esp. around network egress accounting and CDN interplay).
- Slack thread with raw logs: #edge-latency-snapshots (see linked_artifacts)

-- Diego
